t.1.76.1: Then, after a long time, O best of kings, Devayānī, the fair-complexioned lady, went out to that very forest for the sake of play.
t.1.76.2: Then, together with Śarmiṣṭhā and those thousand maidservants, she came to that very same place and roamed about as she pleased, greatly delighted, accompanied by all those companions of hers.
t.1.76.3: All of them, playing and delighting themselves, were drinking the honeyed mādhavī wine, eating various kinds of food, and biting into fruits.
t.1.76.4: And once again King Nāhuṣa, eager for game, came by chance to that very same place, seeking water and worn out with fatigue.
t.1.76.5: He saw Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā, and those women too, drinking and frolicking, adorned with celestial ornaments.
t.1.76.6: And he saw Devayānī of the bright smile seated there, a most excellent woman, peerless in beauty among those women, being served by Śarmiṣṭhā with the massaging of her feet and other attentions.
t.1.76.7: You two maidens are surrounded by two thousand maidens; I ask you both your lineages and your names.
t.1.76.8: Devayānī said: I shall tell you; accept my words, O lord of men. There is one named Śukra, the guru of the Asuras; know me to be his daughter.
t.1.76.9: And this is my friend and servant, who goes wherever I go: Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, lord of the Dānavas.
t.1.76.10: Yayāti said: How is it, O fair-browed one, that this maiden of lovely complexion, the daughter of the lord of the Asuras, is your friend and your slave? Great indeed is my curiosity.
t.1.76.11: All beings, O tiger among men, follow what destiny ordains. Knowing this to be ordained by destiny, do not make all these various arguments.
t.1.76.13: Through my studentship of brahmacarya the entire Veda has come within the path of my hearing. I am a king and the son of a king, renowned by the name Yayāti.
t.1.76.14: Devayānī said: For what purpose, O king, have you come to this place? Is it because you wish to gather some lotus or water-flower, or out of a desire to hunt deer?
t.1.76.12: Your form and dress are like a king's, yet you speak the speech of a brahmin. What is your name, where are you from, and whose son are you? Tell me.
t.1.76.15: Hunting for deer, good lady, I came here in search of water. I have been questioned at length, so please give me leave to go.
t.1.76.17: Know this, O daughter of Uśanas, blessings upon you: I am not worthy of you, O spirited lady; for kings are not fit to marry with your father, O Devayānī.
t.1.76.16: Together with two thousand maidens and with Śarmiṣṭhā as my servant, I am in your power; blessings upon you! Be my friend and my husband.
t.1.76.19: Yayāti said: Though the four classes have sprung from a single body, O lovely lady, they have separate duties and separate rules of purity; and among them the brāhmaṇa is the highest.
t.1.76.18: The kṣatra is joined with the brahman, and the kṣatra is united with the brahman; you are both a seer and a seer's son, so come, Nāhuṣa, wed me.
t.1.76.21: How indeed could another man touch the hand of me, a high-minded woman, a hand that has been taken by the son of a seer, or else by you yourself, a seer?
t.1.76.20: O Nāhuṣa, this rite of taking the hand was never performed with me by men before. You were the first to take my hand, and therefore I choose you.
t.1.76.22: Yayāti said: A man who knows the truth should regard a brahmin as harder to assail than an enraged venomous serpent, or than a blazing fire that faces every way.
t.1.76.24: A venomous serpent kills but one, and by a weapon but one is slain; but a brahmin, when angered, destroys even cities together with their kingdoms.
t.1.76.23: Why do you say, bull among men, that a brahmin is more dangerous to assail than a venomous snake or a fire blazing on every side?
t.1.76.25: A brahmin is, in my view, even harder to assail than that, O timid one; therefore, good lady, I will not marry you unless you are given to me by your father.
t.1.76.26: Marry me, given to you by my father, for you, O king, have been chosen by me. For one who has not asked and who accepts what is given, there is no fear.
t.1.76.28: As soon as he saw Śukra arrive, Yayāti, lord of the earth, standing with joined palms and bowed low, paid homage to the brahmin Kāvya.
t.1.76.27: Then Devayānī swiftly sent word to her own father, and as soon as he heard it, the Bhārgava showed himself to the king.
t.1.76.29: Devayānī said: Father, this is King Nāhuṣa; he took my hand when I was in distress. Homage to you! Give me to him; I choose no other husband in the world.
t.1.76.30: O hero, you have been chosen as husband by this daughter of mine, dear to me; take her, given by me, as your chief queen, O son of Nahuṣa.
t.1.76.32: Śukra said: I release you from the unrighteousness; choose as you wish. Do not be dejected about this marriage; I dispel your sin.
t.1.76.31: So that no great unrighteousness born of the mixing of the classes may touch me here, O Bhārgava, I appeal to you, O brahmin.
t.1.76.33: Take as your wife, in accordance with dharma, the slender-waisted Devayānī; with her you will attain incomparable joy.
t.1.76.34: And this maiden Śarmiṣṭhā, daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, is always to be honored by you, O king, and you must not call her to your bed.
t.1.76.35: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, Yayāti circumambulated Śukra and, permitted by the great-souled one, went joyfully to his own city.
